stories.title: Nalayak: BJP leader lashes out at J&K Police over cops killed in terror attack
stories.summary: Nalayak: BJP leader lashes out at J&K Police over cops killed in terror attack
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'terror attack' in title weight 84
event term: 'terror attack' in summary weight 50.4
article_sentences: The controversial remarks came during the J&K IGP's visit to the remote Dachhan area of Kishtwar district to meet the families of two SPOs killed in a suspected terror attack recently.

A major political controversy erupted in Jammu and Kashmir on Saturday after Leader of Opposition and senior Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) leader Sunil Sharma criticised the police in strong terms, calling the force 'Nalayak' and 'Na-Ahal' in the presence of Inspector General of Police (IGP), Jammu Zone, Tejinder Singh.
The remarks came during the IGP's visit to the remote Dachhan area of Kishtwar district to meet the families of two Special.
Police Officers (SPOs) killed in a suspected terror attack recently.

Sharma, who was accompanied by Kishtwar MLA Shagun Parihar, questioned the police's security arrangements and operational decisions following the killing of SPOs Babi Chand (57) and Rashpal Kumar (45), residents of Kiyar village.
The two personnel went missing on Wednesday while travelling through the mountainous terrain towards a security post at Basnand in the adjoining Marwah tehsil.
Their bullet-riddled bodies were recovered from the Dachhan forest area early Thursday.
During his interaction with the IGP, Sharma questioned why the two SPOs had been sent across a difficult stretch of mountainous terrain to assist Army personnel.
He argued that the deployment exposed them to unnecessary risks and questioned why personnel from nearby police pickets were not assigned the responsibility instead.
"What kind of operational strategy is this?" Sharma asked, expressing concern over what he described as negligence and inadequate planning.
He also questioned the decision to send the SPOs into a sensitive operational area with.303 and INSAS rifles.
The BJP leader further raised concerns over the delay in the security response following the killings.

stories.headline: Cyclone ‘Akvan’ likely to hit AP coast on Nov 18
stories.title: Cyclone ‘Akvan’ likely to hit AP coast on Nov 18
stories.summary: System likely to intensify into a severe cyclonic storm by Wednesday, with winds reaching 120 kmph over the sea Heavy to extremely heavy rainfall forecast for Nov 18 and 19 Exact landfall location yet to be identified; IMD issues orange alert
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Amaravati: Andhra Pradesh is bracing for yet another cyclone as a weather system developing over the Bay of Bengal is expected to intensify into a severe cyclonic storm and move towards the north Andhra coast by November 19.
The approaching system, named ‘Akvan’, is likely to bring heavy to extremely heavy rainfall to several coastal districts on November 18 and 19.
The coastal region is yet to fully recover from the devastation caused by two successive cyclones; therefore, the impending severe cyclonic storm has put the administration on hyper alert.
Managing director of the State Disaster Management Authority Prakhar Jain said a well-marked low-pressure area over the south-eastern Bay of Bengal was moving in a north-northwesterly direction.
It is likely to intensify into a depression by Sunday morning, a deep depression by Monday morning and a cyclonic storm by Monday evening.
The system is subsequently expected to strengthen into a severe cyclonic storm over the central and adjoining west-central Bay of Bengal by Wednesday.
Wind speeds over the sea are likely to reach around 120 kmph as the system intensifies.
Winds of 40–50 kmph, gusting up to 60 kmph, are expected from November 16.
Fishermen who have ventured into the sea have been advised to return to the coast by the evening of November 15.
They have been advised to avoid fishing activity thereafter until the storm passes and weather returns to normal.
Jain said the exact landfall location was yet to be established, as the system was following an “unusual track”, according to current IMD model projections.
The India Meteorological Department and the Cyclone Warning Centre in Visakhapatnam are continuously monitoring its movement and intensity.

stories.headline: Flood-prone areas to be monitored using drones in Chennai
stories.title: Flood-prone areas to be monitored using drones in Chennai
stories.summary: One drone and a trained operating team will be stationed in each of the city’s 15 zones
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Residents in low-lying and flood-prone neighbourhoods across Chennai could be monitored more closely during the Northeast monsoon, with the Greater Chennai Corporation (GCC) planning to deploy drones across all 15 zones for 30 days, to help officials assess conditions on the ground.
The initiative is intended to help civic officials keep track of vulnerable locations during periods of heavy rain and improve coordination of response measures.
Aerial footage will allow officials to assess the situation in areas that may be difficult to monitor from the ground and identify locations requiring attention.
Under the proposed arrangement, one drone and a trained operating team will be stationed in each of the city’s 15 zones, covering the northern, central, and southern regions.
The teams will coordinate with zonal officials on the locations to be monitored and the timing of operations, according to officials.
Live video feeds will be made available to designated GCC officials, while recorded footage will be handed over for subsequent assessment.
The recordings will include details such as the date, time, zone, and location, wherever available.
The footage is expected to support officials in assessing ground conditions in vulnerable neighbourhoods and in coordinating their response during the monsoon.
The deployment will cover 30 days, with the operating teams required to follow the locations and priorities identified by GCC officials.

stories.headline: Intensify counter-insurgency operations: DG CRPF
stories.title: Intensify counter-insurgency operations: DG CRPF
stories.summary: Srinagar, Nov 14: Director General (DG), Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF), G.P. Singh, on Saturday chaired an Operational Conference at Group Centre CRPF Srinagar and instructed senior officers to intensify counter-insurgency operations across the Valley, strengthen the security grid, enhance real-time coordination between security forces and maintain heightened operational readiness to neutralise terrorist elements and their support networks. The conference was attended by Vitul Kumar, SDG (Ops) Directorate; Sandeep Khirwar, SDG, J&K Zone; Vineet Brijlal, IG, Ops Kashmir Sector; Pawan Kumar Sharma, IG Srinagar Sector; other senior officers of the CRPF and ground commanders of Valley-based CRPF units and offices. Discussions focused on the way forward for sustained and intensified counter-insurgency operations in the region. The DG also felicitated troops involved in the twin successful operations "Ops Ashdhar" and "Ops Korag" conducted in Budgam during September 2026, in which two Lashkar-e-Taiba foreign terrorists, Yasir and Hashim Moosa, were neutralised. He appreciated their professionalism, courage under challenging terrain conditions and operational excellence, emphasising that such intelligence-based operations have strengthened the security framework in the region and reinforced the Force's commitment to maintaining peace and stability. The DG's visit to the Kashmir Valley on November 13 and 14 followed the terror attack on CRPF personnel in Kulgam district on November 11. Shortly after landing at Srinagar airport on November 13, he proceeded to the incident site near Nowpora, Akhran in Kulgam, and reviewed the ground situation, security arrangements and the ongoing search operation around the site. Accompanied by senior CRPF officers, the DG visited the Army's 92 Base Hospital in Badami Bagh cantonment and met Head Constable (GD) Sonbir Singh of 46 Battalion CRPF, who is undergoing treatment for serious injuries sustained while responding to the Kulgam attack. He enquired about the jawan's health and treatment, praised his courage and swift retaliation and wished him a speedy recovery. In the evening, the DG attended a security review meeting with senior officers of Jammu and Kashmir Police, the Army and other sister agencies.

stories.headline: After Arnab and Murasu, Andhra Pradesh braces for another cyclonic storm
stories.title: After Arnab and Murasu, Andhra Pradesh braces for another cyclonic storm
stories.summary: Cyclone may make landfall along the North Coastal Andhra Pradesh either on the night of November 19 or in the early hours of November 20, says IMD
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: According to the latest information from the India Meteorological Department (IMD), Amaravati, the current weather system over the Bay of Bengal may intensify into a severe cyclonic storm by November 18, and move towards the Andhra Pradesh coast.
The current weather models indicate the probability of landfall along the North Coastal Andhra Pradesh on November 19 or 20.
The low-pressure area, formed over the south-east Bay of Bengal on November 13, intensified into a well-marked low-pressure area on Saturday.
The weather system is moving northwestwards and may intensify into a depression by November 15.
Thereafter, the system may strengthen into a cyclonic storm over the south and west-central Bay of Bengal around November 16, and further into a severe cyclonic storm on November 18.
The IMD has issued an isolated heavy rainfall alert for Coastal Andhra Pradesh, saying that the forecast may be updated after more clarity emerges.
Wind speeds near the coast may gradually increase from November 15, rising from 40 kmph to 50 kmph and reaching 105 kmph around November 18.

This year, Andhra Pradesh has experienced successive tropical cyclones—very severe cyclonic storm Arnab and severe cyclonic storm Murasu, which made landfall near Narsapur and Ongole, respectively, on the nights of October 28 and November 2.
Two cyclones making landfall within five days is considered rare, and within 18 days after Cyclone Murasu hit the Andhra Pradesh coast, the third cyclonic storm is brewing over the Bay of Bengal.
According to the IMD, Andhra Pradesh has not seen three consecutive cyclones cross its coast within a month since 1970.
“Usually, four tropical cyclones develop over the Bay of Bengal in a year.
This time, they are happening in a row and two of them have hit the A.P. coast,” IMD, Amaravati, Director K. Naga Ratnam told.

stories.headline: Saving Wetlands is Saving Kashmir
stories.title: Saving Wetlands is Saving Kashmir
stories.summary: A wetland rarely disappears in a single dramatic moment. It is edged out, one patch at a time: a stretch filled, a channel narrowed, waste tipped into water, a boundary left unmarked. A little later, the damage is described as inevitable. In Kashmir, where wetlands are woven into the valley’s ecology and daily life, that slow disappearance should alarm us. Saving them is not a sentimental appeal to preserve scenery. It is a practical demand to protect people, livelihoods and the natural systems on which the region depends. The valley’s wetlands are not empty land waiting to be put to use. They are living landscapes—holding water, supporting fish and plants, providing habitat for birds, and helping sustain the communities around them. They also form part of Kashmir’s natural defence against excess water. Wetlands can absorb and store water, easing pressure on settlements and drainage systems during periods of heavy rainfall. Their capacity is not unlimited, and it cannot replace sound planning or infrastructure. But treating them as expendable weakens one of the safeguards nature has already placed in our hands. That is why the loss of a wetland is never confined to its boundary. When a marsh is filled or its waterways are obstructed, the consequences can travel outward: water has fewer places to settle, pollution has fewer natural processes to help absorb it, and habitats become more fragmented. People may notice the change first as an unpleasant smell, declining fish or fewer birds. The deeper cost is less visible—the loss of resilience that becomes apparent when the land is under stress. Kashmir’s wetlands have long been caught between competing pressures. Growing settlements require space, roads and services. Agriculture and other livelihoods depend on land and water. Tourism brings economic opportunity, but also more waste and demand on fragile places. These needs are real. Yet development that erases the ecological foundations of a region is not progress; it is a transfer of costs from the present to the future. A wetland filled today may appear to solve an immediate land-use problem, while leaving residents to bear the consequences of diminished water storage, degraded surroundings and lost livelihoods. The first requirement of protection is to know what exists and where. Wetlands need clear, publicly accessible boundaries, accurate records and regular monitoring. Without those basics, violations can be disputed, enforcement delayed and responsibility passed from one office to another. Mapping must be more than a document produced for a file. It should guide land-use decisions, inform local communities and help officials identify changes before they become irreversible. Where boundaries are already known, they must be marked on the ground and defended consistently. The next requirement is enforcement. Laws and notifications mean little if construction, dumping or filling continue without timely action. Authorities must investigate encroachments, stop ongoing damage and hold violators accountable, regardless of their influence. If a wetland has been illegally altered, restoration should be pursued wherever it is ecologically possible. This cannot mean simply removing visible debris and declaring the matter resolved. Water channels, vegetation, habitats and the relationships between a wetland and its surrounding landscape all matter. Restoration requires expertise, patience and monitoring. Pollution is another front on which protection must become visible. Untreated sewage, solid waste and run-off can degrade water and harm the plants, fish and other life that make wetlands function. Cleaning campaigns may remove litter for a day, but they cannot substitute for reliable waste collection, treatment facilities and enforcement against dumping. Nor should communities living beside wetlands be left to carry a burden created by failures of planning and service delivery. If officials expect people to protect these places, they must provide the systems that make protection possible. The people who live near wetlands should be partners in their conservation, not treated as obstacles to it. Their knowledge of seasonal water, local changes and long-standing uses can help identify problems early. At the same time, conservation plans must recognise legitimate livelihood needs and explain clearly what activities are permitted and why. Rules imposed without consultation can breed resentment; rules enforced selectively invite distrust. Transparent decision-making and meaningful participation are essential to make protection fair as well as effective. This is especially important because the benefits of wetlands extend beyond the villages beside them. The health of a wetland can affect water, wildlife and the wider landscape. Its decline may impose costs on communities that had little say in the decisions that damaged it. Protecting a wetland is therefore a public responsibility. Local bodies, planners, environmental agencies and elected representatives must work from shared information and clear lines of accountability. When authority is divided, coordination cannot be optional: there must be a named body responsible for action, a timetable for review and public reporting on progress. The public, too, has a role—but public participation must not become a convenient excuse for government inaction. Residents can report dumping, support community monitoring and avoid treating wetlands as rubbish grounds. Schools and local organisations can help build awareness of why these landscapes matter. Yet people cannot be expected to compensate for absent sewage treatment, weak enforcement or unplanned construction. Civic responsibility and official responsibility belong together; neither cancels the other. There is also a need to resist the idea that every piece of land must be judged by its immediate commercial value. Wetlands provide benefits that are often not captured in a market price: flood moderation, habitat, water-related livelihoods, public health and a sense of place. Once a wetland is filled, those benefits are difficult—sometimes impossible—to recreate. Decisions about development should therefore account for the cost of losing these functions, not merely the short-term gain from changing the land’s use. Prevention is usually less costly and more reliable than repairing damage after it has spread. Saving wetlands does not mean freezing Kashmir in time or denying communities the infrastructure they need. It means planning with an honest understanding of ecological limits. Roads, housing and public services can be developed while respecting protected areas, provided that rules are clear and alternatives are considered before construction begins. Every proposal affecting a wetland should face careful scrutiny, public disclosure and an assessment of its wider consequences. Where development would cause irreversible harm, the answer should be to find another site—not to make the wetland absorb the cost. The test of commitment will not be how often wetlands appear in speeches. It will be whether boundaries are protected, pollution is reduced, encroachments are stopped and restoration is followed through. It will be whether communities can see the decisions being made and know who is responsible when promises are broken. Conservation succeeds through steady administration as much as through public concern. Kashmir cannot afford to regard wetlands as leftover spaces between settlements. They are part of the region’s living infrastructure, shaped by water and indispensable to the health of the landscape. Their protection demands more than occasional clean-ups or declarations of intent. It requires planning that respects natural systems, enforcement that applies equally and investment in the services that prevent pollution and degradation. The choice is not between people and wetlands. It is between short-term decisions that weaken the valley’s natural safeguards and a form of development that recognises their value. A wetland lost to neglect is not merely a patch of land altered. It is a public asset diminished and a responsibility deferred. Saving these places is, in the most direct sense, saving Kashmir’s capacity to endure. ( The Author is a lecturer in HED and a columnist)

If officials expect people to protect these places, they must provide the systems that make protection possible.
The people who live near wetlands should be partners in their conservation, not treated as obstacles to it.
Their knowledge of seasonal water, local changes and long-standing uses can help identify problems early.
At the same time, conservation plans must recognise legitimate livelihood needs and explain clearly what activities are permitted and why.
Rules imposed without consultation can breed resentment; rules enforced selectively invite distrust.
Transparent decision-making and meaningful participation are essential to make protection fair as well as effective.
This is especially important because the benefits of wetlands extend beyond the villages beside them.
The health of a wetland can affect water, wildlife and the wider landscape.
Its decline may impose costs on communities that had little say in the decisions that damaged it.
Protecting a wetland is therefore a public responsibility.
Local bodies, planners, environmental agencies and elected representatives must work from shared information and clear lines of accountability.
When authority is divided, coordination cannot be optional: there must be a named body responsible for action, a timetable for review and public reporting on progress.
The public, too, has a role—but public participation must not become a convenient excuse for government inaction.
Residents can report dumping, support community monitoring and avoid treating wetlands as rubbish grounds.
Schools and local organisations can help build awareness of why these landscapes matter.
Civic responsibility and official responsibility belong together; neither cancels the other.
There is also a need to resist the idea that every piece of land must be judged by its immediate commercial value.
Wetlands provide benefits that are often not captured in a market price: flood moderation, habitat, water-related livelihoods, public health and a sense of place.
Once a wetland is filled, those benefits are difficult—sometimes impossible—to recreate.
Decisions about development should therefore account for the cost of losing these functions, not merely the short-term gain from changing the land’s use.
Prevention is usually less costly and more reliable than repairing damage after it has spread.
Saving wetlands does not mean freezing Kashmir in time or denying communities the infrastructure they need.
It means planning with an honest understanding of ecological limits.
Roads, housing and public services can be developed while respecting protected areas, provided that rules are clear and alternatives are considered before construction begins.
Every proposal affecting a wetland should face careful scrutiny, public disclosure and an assessment of its wider consequences.
Where development would cause irreversible harm, the answer should be to find another site—not to make the wetland absorb the cost.
The test of commitment will not be how often wetlands appear in speeches.
It will be whether boundaries are protected, pollution is reduced, encroachments are stopped and restoration is followed through.
It will be whether communities can see the decisions being made and know who is responsible when promises are broken.
Conservation succeeds through steady administration as much as through public concern.
Kashmir cannot afford to regard wetlands as leftover spaces between settlements.
They are part of the region’s living infrastructure, shaped by water and indispensable to the health of the landscape.
Their protection demands more than occasional clean-ups or declarations of intent.
It requires planning that respects natural systems, enforcement that applies equally and investment in the services that prevent pollution and degradation.
The choice is not between people and wetlands.
It is between short-term decisions that weaken the valley’s natural safeguards and a form of development that recognises their value.
A wetland lost to neglect is not merely a patch of land altered.
It is a public asset diminished and a responsibility deferred.
Saving these places is, in the most direct sense, saving Kashmir’s capacity to endure.
( The Author is a lecturer in HED and a columnist).
